gloss_terse: young she-camel, dromedary (Arabic cognate: young female camel, valued for speed and vigor)
gloss_readable: This rare feminine noun denotes a young female camel, prized in the ancient Near East for its swiftness and energy. The Arabic cognate bakrah confirms this specialized sense. Jeremiah uses it metaphorically to describe Israel's restless, directionless wandering in pursuit of false gods—a young camel racing back and forth in the wilderness.

senses.1: Refers to a young female camel, emphasized in Jeremiah 2:23 where Israel's spiritual adultery is compared to a swift young camel running wild in the desert. The Spanish 'camella' and English 'young camel' capture the feminine gender and youth that distinguish this term from generic camel words.

gloss_terse: first-ripe fig, early fig (a delicacy, appearing before main harvest)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun specifically designates the first figs to ripen in early summer, considered a delicacy in ancient Israel. The plural form in Jeremiah 24:2 may denote early ripeness as an abstract quality rather than individual fruits. These prized early figs appear in prophecies of judgment (Hosea 9:10) and restoration (Isaiah 28:4), symbolizing either choiceness or vulnerability.

senses.1: Denotes the early-ripening figs valued as seasonal delicacies. In Jeremiah 24:2, the plural 'firstfruits' (English) and 'las tempranas' (Spanish) emphasize the temporal priority and quality of these figs, which serve as a symbol for the exiles who will return to favor with God.

gloss_terse: the Becherite (gentilic adjective: descendant of Becher, son of Ephraim)
gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective with the definite article functions as a collective noun denoting the clan descended from Becher, a son of Ephraim. Numbers 26:35 lists them among the families of Ephraim during the wilderness census. The consistent use of 'Becherite' across translations reflects the standard Hebrew pattern for forming clan names.

senses.1: A collective designation for the descendants of Becher in the census of Numbers 26:35. The definite article with the gentilic form ('the Becherite' in English, 'der Becherite' in German) indicates the entire clan or family group, standard in tribal enumeration lists.

gloss_terse: mind, heart, attention (Aramaic noun for mental faculty or concern)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun denotes the mind or mental faculty, specifically one's attention or concern directed toward a matter. It appears in the idiom 'set mind to' in Daniel 6:14, where King Darius applies his full mental effort to rescuing Daniel from the lions' den. The Syriac and Arabic cognates confirm the semantic field of heart and mental focus.

senses.1: Refers to the mental faculty or deliberate attention in Daniel 6:14. The phrase 'set mind' (English) and 'corazón' (Spanish, heart) show how Darius directed his full cognitive effort toward delivering Daniel, illustrating the king's earnest concern and determination despite political constraints.

gloss_terse: to wear out, wear away, harass continually (Piel: intensively exhaust or oppress)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb in the Piel stem means to wear away or wear out, used figuratively in Daniel 7:25 for relentless harassment or oppression. The related Hebrew root balah conveys similar ideas of decay and exhaustion through attrition. The prophetic context describes an arrogant ruler who will persistently harass God's holy ones.

senses.1: Describes persistent, grinding oppression in Daniel 7:25 where the little horn 'will wear out' the saints of the Most High. The Spanish 'quebrantará' (will break down) and English 'wear out' both capture the notion of exhausting victims through relentless pressure over time.

gloss_terse: Bilgai (personal name: priest who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah)
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies a priest or priestly family head who joined Nehemiah in sealing the covenant renewal in post-exilic Jerusalem. Nehemiah 10:8 lists Bilgai among the leaders who committed themselves and the people to obey God's law. The name may be related to roots suggesting cheerfulness or brightness.

senses.1: Personal name of a priestly leader in Nehemiah 10:8. The consistent transliteration 'Bilgai' across English and Spanish versions reflects the proper noun status, identifying one of the covenant signatories in the post-exilic restoration community.

gloss_terse: Balah (place name: town in the territory of Simeon, possibly same as Baalah)
gloss_readable: This geographical name designates a town allotted to the tribe of Simeon in Joshua 19:3. It may be identical to Baalah (Joshua 15:29) and Bilhah (1 Chronicles 4:29), representing variant spellings or forms of the same settlement. The site's exact location remains uncertain, somewhere in the southern Negev region.

senses.1: Denotes a Simeonite town in Joshua 19:3. The conjunction 'and Balah' (English, German) and 'y Bala' (Spanish) simply links this place name in the territorial boundary list, with minor spelling variations across manuscripts reflecting phonetic equivalence.

gloss_terse: to trouble, disturb, frighten (Piel participle: those troubling them in building)
gloss_readable: This verb means to trouble, disturb, or intimidate, appearing in Ezra 4:4 as a Piel participle describing local adversaries who 'were troubling' the Jewish returnees during temple reconstruction. The Ketiv (written) form uses this root, while the Qere (read) substitutes the more common bahal. Both roots convey fear and disruption.

senses.1: Describes active intimidation and harassment in Ezra 4:4, where opponents 'troubled them in building' the temple. The Spanish 'aterrorizándolos' (terrorizing them) captures the sustained campaign of psychological warfare and obstruction aimed at halting the reconstruction project.

gloss_terse: Bilhah (place name: town in Simeon, likely same as Baalah and Balah)
gloss_readable: This place name appears in 1 Chronicles 4:29 as a Simeonite settlement, probably identical to Baalah (Joshua 15:29) and Balah (Joshua 19:3), representing orthographic variants of the same town. The uncertainty about the site's identification reflects the textual variations and the challenge of locating small settlements in the Negev after centuries of shifting populations.

senses.1: Geographic designation in 1 Chronicles 4:29 for a Simeonite town. The prepositional phrase 'and in Bilhah' marks this as one location in a series of settlements, with the variant spelling reflecting manuscript traditions or dialectal differences in pronouncing the town's name.

gloss_terse: to curb, hold in, restrain (used of controlling animals with bit and bridle)
gloss_readable: This verb means to curb or restrain, appearing as an infinitive in Psalm 32:9 in the context of controlling animals with bit and bridle. The imagery warns against being like a stubborn horse or mule that requires forceful restraint. The Aramaic cognates confirm the semantic range of holding back or checking unruly behavior.

senses.1: Refers to the restraining action of bit and bridle in Psalm 32:9. The English 'to restrain' and Spanish 'para sujetar' (to subject/control) both capture the coercive control needed for animals lacking understanding, serving as a negative example for how humans should respond to God's guidance.

gloss_terse: to gather figs, tend sycamore trees (technical term for nipping sycamore fruit to ripen it)
gloss_readable: This denominative verb describes the specialized agricultural practice of tending sycamore fig trees, specifically the technique of nipping or piercing the fruit to accelerate ripening and improve flavor. Amos 7:14 uses the participle 'dresser of sycamores' to describe his humble occupation before his prophetic calling. The Greek and Latin versions confirm this technical agricultural sense.

senses.1: Denotes the specialized work of tending sycamore figs in Amos 7:14. The English 'dresser of' and Spanish 'cultivador de' (cultivator of) describe Amos's occupation as one who performed the technical task of nipping sycamore fruit, emphasizing his humble, non-professional origins as a prophet.

gloss_terse: the Belaite (gentilic: descendant of Bela, son of Benjamin)
gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective with the definite article functions collectively to designate the clan descended from Bela, the firstborn son of Benjamin. Numbers 26:38 includes them in the census of Benjaminite families during the wilderness period. The standard transliteration across languages reflects the conventional pattern for forming and translating Hebrew tribal designations.

senses.1: Collective designation for Bela's descendants in the Benjaminite census of Numbers 26:38. The definite article with the gentilic form ('the Belaite' in English and German) marks this as a recognized family group within Benjamin's tribal structure.

gloss_terse: Bileam (place name: Levitical town in Manasseh, same as Ibleam)
gloss_readable: This geographical name designates a Levitical city in the territory of Manasseh, appearing in 1 Chronicles 6:70. It is identical to Ibleam mentioned in Joshua 17:11 and other passages, with the variant spelling likely reflecting dialectal pronunciation. Modern scholarship identifies it with Khirbet Belʿame, north of modern Nablus.

senses.1: Names a Levitical town in Manasseh in 1 Chronicles 6:70. The transliteration 'Bileam' represents an alternate form of 'Ibleam,' showing how the same settlement could be spelled differently in various biblical sources, a common phenomenon with place names in ancient texts.

gloss_terse: Belshazzar (personal name: last Babylonian king in Daniel, son of Nabonidus)
gloss_readable: This Babylonian royal name (Bel-shar-usur, 'Bel, protect the king') identifies the ruler whose feast was interrupted by the handwriting on the wall in Daniel 5. While Daniel presents him as Nebuchadnezzar's successor and son, cuneiform inscriptions reveal he was actually the son of Nabonidus and served as prince regent, not sole king.

senses.1: Personal name of the Babylonian ruler in Daniel 8:1 and throughout chapters 5-8. The transliterations vary slightly across languages but consistently preserve the Babylonian theophoric element 'Bel,' marking this as a foreign royal name tied to Babylon's patron deity and the dramatic judgment narrative.

gloss_terse: high place (cultic worship site, often illicit; also poetically mountaintop or elevated terrain)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun primarily denotes a high place used for worship, often condemned as sites of illicit Canaanite-influenced cult practices, though occasionally referring to legitimate sanctuaries before the temple. The term appears over 100 times, frequently in prophetic denunciations. It also functions poetically to describe mountain heights or elevated terrain, as in 'the high places of the earth' meaning mountain peaks.

senses.1: In Ezekiel 20:29, the term functions as a wordplay (bama/'what/come?') in God's rhetorical question about Israel's continued use of illicit worship sites. The multilingual glosses show translators struggling between transliterating the technical term ('Bamah') and explaining its cultic function ('high place'), highlighting its specialized religious vocabulary.

gloss_terse: Bimhal (personal name: descendant of Asher)
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies a descendant of Asher listed in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles 7:33. The name may derive from 'son of circumcision' according to BDB's etymological suggestion, though such folk etymologies remain uncertain. It appears only in this genealogical context without additional narrative information.

senses.1: Personal name in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:33. The conjunction 'and Bimhal' simply links this name in the family tree, with consistent transliteration across languages marking it as a proper noun without semantic translation.

gloss_terse: Ben (personal name: Levite musician, possibly shortened form; Septuagint omits)
gloss_readable: This simple personal name ('son') identifies a Levite in 1 Chronicles 15:18, though the Septuagint omits it, suggesting possible textual corruption or abbreviation. It may represent a shortened form of a longer theophoric name. The unusual brevity has led some scholars to question whether this is a complete name or a scribal error.

senses.1: Personal name of a Levite in 1 Chronicles 15:18. While translations render it literally as 'Ben' (English) or 'son' (German 'Sohn,' French 'fils'), its status as a proper noun in this context is signaled by capitalization and position in the list, despite its identical form to the common word for 'son.'

gloss_terse: Ben-Oni (personal name: 'son of my sorrow,' Rachel's name for Benjamin before she died)
gloss_readable: This compound personal name means 'son of my sorrow' and represents Rachel's dying choice for her newborn son in Genesis 35:18. The name captured her mortal anguish in childbirth. Jacob immediately renamed the child Benjamin ('son of the right hand'), transforming the memorial of grief into one of blessing and honor, a poignant detail in the patriarchal narrative.

senses.1: Names Rachel's son in her final breath in Genesis 35:18. The meaning 'son of my sorrow' encapsulates the tragedy of her death in childbirth. All major translations preserve the transliteration 'Ben-Oni,' allowing the Hebrew wordplay between the mother's sorrowful name and the father's hopeful renaming to remain visible.

gloss_terse: Ben-Zoheth (personal name: member of Judah's tribe, possibly 'son of Zoheth')
gloss_readable: This compound personal name appears in 1 Chronicles 4:20 in a genealogical list of Judah's descendants. The name structure suggests 'son of Zoheth,' though the relationship to the preceding name Zoheth in the same verse creates interpretive challenges—they may be brothers rather than father and son. The genealogical context provides no additional narrative details.

senses.1: Personal name in Judah's genealogy in 1 Chronicles 4:20. The conjunction 'and Ben-Zoheth' links this figure in the family line. The consistent transliteration across languages preserves the compound Hebrew form, though the relationship between Zoheth and Ben-Zoheth in the same verse remains textually ambiguous.

gloss_terse: Ben-Hail (personal name: 'son of might/valor,' prince under Jehoshaphat who taught the law)
gloss_readable: This compound name means 'son of might' or 'man of valor' and identifies one of the princes whom King Jehoshaphat sent throughout Judah to teach the law to the people (2 Chronicles 17:7). The name reflects the positive virtue of strength and courage. His inclusion in the teaching mission shows that Jehoshaphat enlisted capable leaders for this religious reform.

senses.1: Personal name of one of Jehoshaphat's teaching princes in 2 Chronicles 17:7. The prepositional phrase 'to Ben-Hail' marks him as a recipient of the king's commission to travel through Judah instructing the people in the law, part of a broader religious and educational reform program.

gloss_terse: Ben-Hanan (personal name: 'son of the gracious one,' member of Judah's tribe)
gloss_readable: This compound personal name appears in the genealogical records of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:20. The name likely means 'son of the gracious one' or 'son of Hanan,' reflecting the common Hebrew practice of forming names with ben ('son') plus a divine attribute or ancestor's name. No additional narrative information about this individual survives.

senses.1: Personal name in Judah's genealogy in 1 Chronicles 4:20. Transliterated consistently as 'Ben-Hanan' or variations like 'Ben-Janan' (Spanish), the name appears in a genealogical list without further biographical details, serving simply to preserve family lineage records.

gloss_terse: Ben-Hesed (personal name: 'son of mercy/kindness,' one of Solomon's twelve district officers)
gloss_readable: This compound name meaning 'son of mercy' or 'son of kindness' identifies one of Solomon's twelve district officers responsible for provisioning the royal court (1 Kings 4:10). Each officer supplied provisions for one month per year. The name's meaning reflects positive theological virtues of divine grace and covenant loyalty (hesed).

senses.1: Personal name of a Solomonic administrative officer in 1 Kings 4:10. The consistent transliteration 'Ben-Hesed' across languages preserves the Hebrew compound form, identifying one of the twelve officials who managed the complex logistics of supplying Solomon's extensive royal household and court.

gloss_terse: Bene-Berak (place name: 'sons of lightning,' town in Dan's territory)
gloss_readable: This geographical name means 'sons of lightning' and designates a town allotted to the tribe of Dan in Joshua 19:45. Assyrian records mention Banai-barqa, confirming the site's historical existence. Modern identification places it at Ibn Ibraq (or Ibraq), about an hour southeast of Jaffa, in the coastal plain region.

senses.1: Place name in Dan's tribal allotment in Joshua 19:45. The conjunction 'and Bene-Berak' links this town in the boundary list. Minor spelling variations ('Bene-berac' in Spanish) reflect phonetic equivalence, while the 'sons of lightning' etymology may reference storm phenomena or a local deity.

gloss_terse: building, structure (feminine noun for constructed edifice)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes a building or structure, appearing in Ezekiel 41:13 within the prophet's detailed vision of the restored temple complex. The term refers to a specific constructed edifice, distinct from the general verbal noun binyan. Ezekiel's architectural precision uses this word to designate one component of the elaborate temple vision.

senses.1: Refers to a specific building structure in Ezekiel's temple vision in Ezekiel 41:13. The definite article 'the building' (English, Spanish 'el edificio') marks this as a particular architectural feature in the complex measurements and descriptions that characterize Ezekiel 40-48, where precise temple layout dominates.

gloss_terse: building (Aramaic masculine noun for edifice or construction)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic masculine noun means building or construction, appearing in the emphatic state in Ezra 5:4. The context involves Persian officials questioning the Jewish community about who authorized the temple reconstruction project. The term refers generally to any edifice or built structure, parallel to the Hebrew binyan.

senses.1: Denotes the temple construction project in Ezra 5:4, where Persian authorities demand to know 'Who are the men building this building?' The Aramaic emphatic form marks this as the specific edifice under scrutiny—the Jerusalem temple whose reconstruction had become a point of political concern.

gloss_terse: Beninu (personal name: 'our son,' Levite who sealed Nehemiah's covenant)
gloss_readable: This personal name appears to mean 'our son' and identifies a Levite who joined in sealing the covenant renewal under Nehemiah's leadership (Nehemiah 10:13). The name form suggests a plural possessive construction. He was among the leaders who committed themselves and the community to faithful observance of the law in post-exilic Jerusalem.

senses.1: Personal name of a Levite covenant-sealer in Nehemiah 10:13. Transliterated as 'Beninu' across major versions, the name appears in the list of leaders who formalized the community's renewed commitment to Torah observance after the exile, part of Nehemiah's broader religious and social reforms.

gloss_terse: to be angry, enraged (Aramaic verb for becoming furious)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb means to be angry or enraged, appearing in Daniel 2:12 describing King Nebuchadnezzar's violent reaction when his wise men could not reveal and interpret his dream. The Aramaic root and its cognates in Syriac and Samaritan convey intense anger. The verse combines this verb with 'greatly enraged' to emphasize the king's explosive fury.

senses.1: Describes Nebuchadnezzar's explosive anger in Daniel 2:12 when his counselors failed him. The English 'was enraged' and Spanish 'se enojó' (became angry) capture the king's dangerous fury that led to his death decree against all the wise men of Babylon, setting up Daniel's intervention.

gloss_terse: Ben-Ammi (personal name: 'son of my people,' Lot's son by his younger daughter, ancestor of Ammonites)
gloss_readable: This compound name meaning 'son of my people' identifies the child born from Lot's incestuous relationship with his younger daughter after Sodom's destruction (Genesis 19:38). The name became the eponymous ancestor of the Ammonites (bene ammon, 'sons of Ammon'). The naming represents the mother's claim to preserve her people's lineage, albeit through shameful means.

senses.1: Personal name of Lot's son in Genesis 19:38, ancestor of the Ammonites. The name's meaning 'son of my people' reflects the desperate circumstances and ethnic preservation motive behind the incestuous union. Consistent transliteration across languages preserves the Hebrew form and its etymological connection to 'Ammon.'

gloss_terse: Besodeiah (personal name: 'in the secret/counsel of Yah,' helped repair Jerusalem's wall)
gloss_readable: This theophoric personal name likely means 'in the secret of Yahweh' or 'in Yah's counsel' and identifies one of the builders who helped Nehemiah repair Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah 3:6). The name suggests intimacy with divine wisdom or being privy to God's plans. He participated in the crucial post-exilic reconstruction of Jerusalem's defenses.

senses.1: Personal name of a wall-builder in Nehemiah 3:6. Transliterated consistently as 'Besodeiah' or 'Besodías' (Spanish), the name identifies one of the many volunteers who joined the collaborative effort to restore Jerusalem's walls, each family or individual taking responsibility for specific sections.

gloss_terse: unripe grapes, sour grapes (collectively: grapes not yet ripened or sweet)
gloss_readable: This masculine noun (used collectively) denotes unripe or sour grapes, appearing in prophetic oracles and wisdom literature. Jeremiah 31:29-30 and Ezekiel 18:2 use the proverb about eating sour grapes and children's teeth being set on edge to discuss generational guilt. Job 15:33 employs it metaphorically for premature loss. The term contrasts with ripe, sweet fruit.

senses.1: Refers to immature grapes in Job 15:33 with the third masculine singular suffix ('his unripe grapes'). The metaphor describes the wicked person who loses his fruit prematurely, like a vine dropping its unripe grapes before they can mature and ripen, symbolizing unfulfilled potential and divine judgment.

gloss_terse: ruin, heap of ruins (poetic term for devastation and desolation)
gloss_readable: This masculine noun means ruin or heap of ruins, used poetically to describe devastation. Job 30:24 employs it in a difficult verse describing divine judgment or calamity. The term appears in prophetic oracles depicting cities reduced to rubble. The Aramaic form 'iyyim appears in some texts, showing lexical overlap between Hebrew and Aramaic vocabulary in poetic contexts.

senses.1: Denotes a heap of ruins in Job 30:24 within a challenging poetic passage. The prepositional phrase 'against heap/ruin' appears in Job's lament about suffering and mortality. The Spanish 'contra ruina' and English 'against heap' preserve the stark imagery of destruction, though the verse's exact sense remains debated by interpreters.

gloss_terse: Baal-Hamon (place name: 'possessor of abundance,' location of Solomon's vineyard in Song of Songs)
gloss_readable: This compound place name means 'possessor of abundance' or 'Baal of the multitude' and appears only in Song of Songs 8:11 as the location of Solomon's vineyard. The first element 'Baal' may be the divine name or simply 'possessor/lord.' The site's identification remains uncertain. The context emphasizes the vineyard's great value and productivity.

senses.1: Names the location of Solomon's valuable vineyard in Song of Songs 8:11. The prepositional phrase 'in Baal-Hamon' situates this wealthy agricultural property, whose abundant production contrasts with the Shulammite's personal vineyard. The place name's meaning 'possessor of abundance' may be descriptive or etymological wordplay.

gloss_terse: Baal-Hazor (place name: 'possessor of a court/village,' site where Absalom killed Amnon)
gloss_readable: This compound geographical name meaning 'Baal of the court' or 'possessor of an enclosure' identifies the location where Absalom held the sheep-shearing feast that became the occasion for murdering his brother Amnon (2 Samuel 13:23). It was situated on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin. Possible identification with Tell Asur, though not certain.

senses.1: Names the site of Absalom's revenge in 2 Samuel 13:23. The prepositional phrase 'in Baal-Hazor' locates the sheep-shearing feast where Absalom orchestrated Amnon's assassination two years after the rape of Tamar. The place name marks this location as the setting for a pivotal moment in David's family tragedy.

gloss_terse: owner, lord, husband, master (common noun denoting possessor or one having authority)
gloss_readable: This masculine noun fundamentally means owner or possessor, extending to lord, husband, and master depending on context. It denotes legal ownership (owner of an ox, house, pit) or relationship authority (husband, master). In Hosea 2:16, God declares Israel will call him 'my husband' rather than 'my Baal,' playing on the term's dual meaning as both 'husband' and the rival deity's name.

senses.1: In Hosea 2:16, 'my Baal' functions as a deliberate double entendre. God says Israel will abandon calling Him 'Baali' (my master/Baal) and instead use 'Ishi' (my husband), purging the vocabulary of pagan associations. The multilingual glosses struggle to capture this wordplay between legitimate meaning (master, husband) and idolatrous connotations.

gloss_terse: Beeliada (personal name: 'Baal knows,' original name of David's son, later changed to Eliada)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name meaning 'Baal knows' was originally given to one of David's sons born in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 14:7). The name was later changed to Eliada ('God knows') in 2 Samuel 5:16, substituting El for Baal to remove the pagan deity's name. This name change reflects growing sensitivity about using 'Baal' in Israelite names.

senses.1: Personal name of David's son in 1 Chronicles 14:7, representing the original form before religious revision. The conjunction 'and Beeliada' lists him among David's Jerusalem-born children. The name's Baal element, acceptable in early Israel, was later deemed problematic, leading to the substitution preserved in Samuel's parallel account.

gloss_terse: Bealiah (personal name: 'Yahweh is lord,' warrior who joined David at Ziklag)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name means 'Yahweh is lord' and identifies one of the warriors who defected to David while he was at Ziklag, still in exile from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:5). These Benjaminite warriors were ambidextrous archers and slingers. The name affirms divine lordship, contrasting with Baal-compound names by using the Yahweh element.

senses.1: Personal name of a warrior in David's growing coalition in 1 Chronicles 12:6. The conjunction 'and Baaliah' lists him among the skilled Benjaminite fighters who recognized David's legitimacy before his kingship was established, representing early supporters who proved crucial to David's eventual success.

gloss_terse: Baale-Judah (place name: 'lords/heights of Judah,' alternate name for Kiriath-jearim)
gloss_readable: This geographical designation meaning 'Baals of Judah' or 'lords of Judah' is an alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, appearing in 2 Samuel 6:2 when David retrieved the ark from there. The name may reference earlier Baal worship at the high place or simply mean 'heights/citizens of Judah.' It's identified with the same location as Kiriath-baal and Kiriath-jearim.

senses.1: Names the location where David went to retrieve the ark in 2 Samuel 6:2. The prepositional phrase 'from Baale-Judah' identifies the starting point of the ark's journey to Jerusalem. The Baal element may recall the site's pre-Israelite cultic associations or simply denote 'possessors/citizens of Judah' as a territorial designation.

gloss_terse: Baalis (personal name: king of Ammon who conspired to assassinate Gedaliah)
gloss_readable: This personal name (possibly meaning 'son of delight') identifies the Ammonite king who sent Ishmael to assassinate Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah after Jerusalem's fall (Jeremiah 40:14). His conspiracy succeeded, leading to Gedaliah's murder and further destabilization of the post-586 BC remnant community. Some manuscripts read 'Baalim' instead.

senses.1: Personal name of the Ammonite king in Jeremiah 40:14 who orchestrated Gedaliah's assassination. Transliterated as 'Baalis' in most versions, this foreign ruler exploited Judah's weakness after the exile to pursue Ammonite political interests, contributing to the chaos that drove many Jews to flee to Egypt.

gloss_terse: Baal-Shalishah (place name: location near Gilgal that sent firstfruits to Elisha)
gloss_readable: This compound place name appears in 2 Kings 4:42 as the origin of a man who brought firstfruits bread to Elisha during a famine. The name may mean 'Baal of the three' or 'Baal of Shalishah.' It was located in Ephraim near Gilgal. The LXX renders it Baithsarisath, and it was approximately 15 miles from Diospolis according to Eusebius.

senses.1: Names the source of the bread offering in 2 Kings 4:42. The prepositional phrase 'from Baal-Shalishah' identifies where the man traveled from to bring twenty loaves of barley and fresh grain to Elisha, who miraculously multiplied it to feed a hundred men, foreshadowing Jesus' feeding miracles.

gloss_terse: Baalath-Beer (place name: 'mistress of a well,' also called Ramath-Negeb, town in Simeon)
gloss_readable: This compound geographical name means 'mistress of a well' or 'lady of the well' and designates a town in Simeon's territory, also called Ramath-Negeb (Joshua 19:8). The dual naming reflects either two names for one site or the merger of previously distinct locations. The well reference indicates its significance as a water source in the Negev region.

senses.1: Names a Simeonite settlement in Joshua 19:8. Transliterated consistently as 'Baalath-Beer' across languages, the compound name emphasizes the well that made this location viable in the arid Negev. Its alternate name 'Ramath-Negeb' (height of the south) suggests elevated terrain near a water source.

gloss_terse: the Becherite (gentilic adjective: descendant of Becher, son of Ephraim)
gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective with the definite article functions as a collective noun denoting the clan descended from Becher, a son of Ephraim. Numbers 26:35 lists them among the families of Ephraim during the wilderness census. The consistent use of 'Becherite' across translations reflects the standard Hebrew pattern for forming clan names.

senses.1: A collective designation for the descendants of Becher in the census of Numbers 26:35. The definite article with the gentilic form ('the Becherite' in English, 'der Becherite' in German) indicates the entire clan or family group, standard in tribal enumeration lists.

gloss_terse: mind, heart, attention (Aramaic noun for mental faculty or concern)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun denotes the mind or mental faculty, specifically one's attention or concern directed toward a matter. It appears in the idiom 'set mind to' in Daniel 6:14, where King Darius applies his full mental effort to rescuing Daniel from the lions' den. The Syriac and Arabic cognates confirm the semantic field of heart and mental focus.

senses.1: Refers to the mental faculty or deliberate attention in Daniel 6:14. The phrase 'set mind' (English) and 'corazón' (Spanish, heart) show how Darius directed his full cognitive effort toward delivering Daniel, illustrating the king's earnest concern and determination despite political constraints.

gloss_terse: to wear out, wear away, harass continually (Piel: intensively exhaust or oppress)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb in the Piel stem means to wear away or wear out, used figuratively in Daniel 7:25 for relentless harassment or oppression. The related Hebrew root balah conveys similar ideas of decay and exhaustion through attrition. The prophetic context describes an arrogant ruler who will persistently harass God's holy ones.

senses.1: Describes persistent, grinding oppression in Daniel 7:25 where the little horn 'will wear out' the saints of the Most High. The Spanish 'quebrantará' (will break down) and English 'wear out' both capture the notion of exhausting victims through relentless pressure over time.

gloss_terse: Bilgai (personal name: priest who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah)
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies a priest or priestly family head who joined Nehemiah in sealing the covenant renewal in post-exilic Jerusalem. Nehemiah 10:8 lists Bilgai among the leaders who committed themselves and the people to obey God's law. The name may be related to roots suggesting cheerfulness or brightness.

senses.1: Personal name of a priestly leader in Nehemiah 10:8. The consistent transliteration 'Bilgai' across English and Spanish versions reflects the proper noun status, identifying one of the covenant signatories in the post-exilic restoration community.

gloss_terse: Balah (place name: town in the territory of Simeon, possibly same as Baalah)
gloss_readable: This geographical name designates a town allotted to the tribe of Simeon in Joshua 19:3. It may be identical to Baalah (Joshua 15:29) and Bilhah (1 Chronicles 4:29), representing variant spellings or forms of the same settlement. The site's exact location remains uncertain, somewhere in the southern Negev region.

senses.1: Denotes a Simeonite town in Joshua 19:3. The conjunction 'and Balah' (English, German) and 'y Bala' (Spanish) simply links this place name in the territorial boundary list, with minor spelling variations across manuscripts reflecting phonetic equivalence.
